html:
The Atlanta campaign was fought from 7 May to 2 September 1864 across northwest Georgia, United States, and ended with the capture of Atlanta. A Union force of about 100,000 under General William T. Sherman beat the Confederate Army of Tennessee, led first by Joseph Johnston and then by John Bell Hood.

In 1864 Ulysses S. Grant ordered all Union armies to attack at once, so the Confederacy could not shift troops. Atlanta was Sherman's target: a railway centre with arms factories. He followed the rail line south from Chattanooga. He kept going round Johnston's side instead of attacking, and Johnston fell back. In July the Confederate president replaced Johnston with Hood, who attacked three times in nine days and lost heavily. Sherman then cut the last railway, Hood left on 1 September and Union troops marched in the next day.

The news helped Abraham Lincoln win re-election in November, which meant the American Civil War would be fought to the end. Sherman then marched 60,000 men about 460 km to the sea at Savannah, living off the land and wrecking railways and farms. This March to the Sea was meant to break the South's will to fight.
